title: Getting started
markdown:
## **Register an account**

Everyone who uses the platform should register their own account. Recommended registration practices:
- **Username:** Use an English name, the pinyin of your name, an employee ID, or a phone number. Usernames must be globally unique.
- **Nickname:** Use the name your colleagues normally call you, such as your real name, a familiar nickname, or an English name. This makes it easier to identify the right person when managing permissions or collaborating.
- **Email:** Use your internal company email address.

## **Create or join a Workspace**

### **Onboard a new project**

To onboard a project, create a new Workspace. Each project is isolated in its own Workspace. Here, a project means an independent system, such as a corporate website, supply chain management system, or visitor management system. One project can contain any number of frontend and backend Git repositories.

### **Join an existing project**

If someone on your team has already created the Workspace, you can join it in either of two ways:
1. Switch to “All Workspaces” on the Workspace list page, find the Workspace, and select “Request access”. A Workspace administrator approves the request in “Member management”.
2. Ask a Workspace administrator (the creator or a member with administrator access) to search for your nickname or login name in “Member management” and add you.

## **Use the platform**

### **Connect an Agent to the platform**

Open “Profile settings” at the top right, select “MCP tokens”, and create an MCP token. Configure this MCP connection in Claude Code / Codex CLI / Cursor CLI / Gemini CLI. You can then use Claude Code / Codex CLI / Cursor CLI / Gemini CLI to operate the platform: create Requirements, analyze Delivery errors, or configure Squads, Agents, SDLC workflows, repositories, and Executors. CodeFlow is AI Native; we recommend using an Agent for complex and repetitive operations.

![MCP client configuration](/help/assets/02-en-US.png "")

After configuring MCP, ask your Agent to “Use CodeFlow MCP to operate the ‘XXX’ Workspace”. We recommend installing the `ainative.zip` Skill in your Agent tool. For later operations on CodeFlow, enter `/ainative` in the Agent.

[ainative.zip](/help/assets/ainative.zip)

The Skill content is shown below. It instructs your Agent to use the CodeFlow platform MCP to perform operations.
```markdown
---
name: ainative
description: Use when the user invokes ainative or asks to perform an operation through the CodeFlow platform.
---

# CodeFlow

Use the CodeFlow platform MCP to perform operations.

```

Example: ask `/ainative` to analyze whether the Agents, their SDLC definitions, repository configuration, repository relationships, and Agent repository bindings in the Standard Automated Delivery Squad of the “XXX” Workspace are complete. Ask whether the Squad can deliver Requirements automatically, which stages hand off automatically, and which need human intervention.
```markdown
/ainative Analyze whether the Agents, their SDLC definitions, repository configuration, repository relationships, and Agent repository bindings in the Standard Automated Delivery Squad of the "XXX" Workspace are complete. Can the entire Squad deliver Requirements automatically? Which stages hand off automatically, and which require human intervention?
```

**Project administrators:** If you administer a project Workspace and are responsible for onboarding the project, configure its Squads, Agents, SDLC workflows, repositories, and repository relationships for the actual project. This defines the AI automated Delivery pipeline and is a critical step best performed by someone who knows the project well. Continue to optimize, iterate on, and maintain the configuration to improve Delivery efficiency and quality and reduce token consumption. See the “Project onboarding” chapter for configuration instructions.

**Project team members:** If you work on development or testing and are responsible for Delivery, focus on the “Requirements”, “Scheduled tasks”, and “Execution records” modules in the Delivery section to submit, clarify, and deliver requirements.

title: Project onboarding
markdown:
## **Setup steps**

### Step 1: Create a project Workspace

Create a new Workspace for the project.

### Step 2: Get the source and initialize templates

#### Get the project source

Clone the CodeFlow source locally using the following commands. Git sparse checkout downloads only the CodeFlow project source. If `git clone` is unavailable, download the source from Git instead: [https://github.com/qsumm/CodeFlow](https://github.com/qsumm/CodeFlow).

```markdown
git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout \
https://github.com/qsumm/CodeFlow.git

cd CodeFlow

git sparse-checkout init --no-cone

git sparse-checkout set /platform/ainative/

git checkout master
```

#### Set the Agent working directory

Create a session in Claude Code / Codex CLI / Cursor CLI / Gemini CLI and set its working directory to `ainative/platform/ainative`. This lets Claude Code / Codex CLI / Cursor CLI / Gemini CLI discover the template initialization Skill in the CodeFlow source.

#### Initialize Workspace templates

Use the prompt below to initialize templates. The `initialize-ainative-harness` Skill in the CodeFlow source imports templates containing Squads, Agents, and SDLC workflows into your Workspace. Templates make initial onboarding easier; once familiar with the platform, you can configure a project entirely yourself. A Flash model is sufficient; the Skill is expected to take about 20 minutes. Prerequisite: **the Agent must already be connected to CodeFlow through MCP**.

The example asks the Skill to initialize all templates in the “XXX” Workspace.
```markdown
/initialize-ainative-harness Initialize all templates in the "XXX" Workspace.
```

**Example names:** The examples below use Quick Delivery Squad, Standard Automated Delivery Squad, Requirements Clarification, Quick Full-Stack Developer, Quick Deployment Engineer, and Project Manager. When working with your own configuration, refer to the actual Squad and Agent names in your Workspace.

### Step 3: Adapt templates to your project

#### Analyze template variables

After initialization, enter the following prompt in the same session. It asks the Agent to use CodeFlow MCP for the “XXX” Workspace and identify the `{{}}` variables in the Agents and SDLC definitions of “Quick Delivery Squad”. The initialized configuration is still the default template and needs project-specific values.

```markdown
For the rest of this session, use CodeFlow MCP to operate the "XXX" Workspace on the CodeFlow platform:
- Identify the variables in the Agents and their SDLC definitions in the Quick Delivery Squad. The Squad still uses the default initialized templates with variables in {{}} format. I need to update this configuration for my project.
```

#### Update the template configuration

Replace the identified variables with your project's actual information. Describe the project to the Agent and ask it to analyze and update the template configuration. The example covers:

- **Deployment:** If using Jenkins, explain that deployment triggering is packaged as a Skill uploaded to the Workspace, give its name “XXX”, and provide `ProjectID` and `JobID`. Ask the Agent to trigger deployment with that Skill. For local testing and deployment, select an unused random port between 18000 and 19000 to avoid conflicts between branches. Check whether the port is occupied before deployment and choose another in that range if necessary.
- **Database:** Provide the database version (MySQL 8.0 in the example), username `dev_user`, password `xxx`, and connection address and port `xxx`.
- **Branch merging before deployment:** If required, ask the Agent to merge the development branch into `dev` before deployment. If CICD receives branch information and merges it in the deployment pipeline, remove the branch-merging variables and explain that arrangement. Configure other cases according to the actual required stage and logic.

```markdown
# Update deployment information
For example, if your deployment environment uses Jenkins:
- My deployment environment is Jenkins. I have packaged its deployment trigger as a Skill and uploaded it to the Workspace. The Skill is named "XXX". Use this Skill to trigger deployment, with ProjectID set to XXX and JobID set to XXX.
If your project tests require a local startup, you can say:
My project is tested and validated locally, and deployment means starting it locally. To avoid port conflicts when multiple branches are deployed locally, randomly select a port between 18000 and 19000. Before deployment, check whether the selected port is occupied; if it is, choose another port in the same range.

# Update database information
My database is MySQL 8.0. The username is dev_user, the password is xxx, and the connection address and port are xxx.

# Merge branches before deployment
If you need to merge into dev before deployment, say: Merge the current development branch into dev before deployment.
If you pass branch information to the deployment pipeline and CICD merges it automatically, say: Remove the branch-merging variables. My deployment passes the current development branch to the CICD pipeline, which performs the merge.
For other arrangements, configure the branch-merging stage and logic according to your actual requirements.

```

Give this information to the Agent so it can combine the variable analysis and actual project details to update the configuration.

### Step 4: Configure repositories and MCP

#### Configure repositories and their relationships

Describe all project repositories and their relationships to the Agent so it can configure and associate them. The sample prompt asks it to configure the repositories and descriptions, set their relationships, bind every repository to every Agent with `Write` permission, and automatically publish and approve the Agents afterward.

The sample uses four `https://gitlab.com/xxx.git` repositories with the `master` default branch: the backend repository contains Java backend business code; the frontend repository contains Vue client code; the API repository contains Java interface definitions; and the middleware repository contains Java database and Redis code. The frontend depends on the backend, which depends on the API and middleware repositories.

```markdown
Configure the following repository information and descriptions in my project Workspace, and configure the repository relationships provided below. Then bind all repositories to every Agent with Write permission, and automatically publish and approve the Agents.

Project repositories:
Backend repository: https://gitlab.com/xxx.git, default branch: master
Frontend repository: https://gitlab.com/xxx.git, default branch: master
API repository: https://gitlab.com/xxx.git, default branch: master
Middleware repository: https://gitlab.com/xxx.git, default branch: master

Repository descriptions:
The backend repository contains the project's Java server code. Develop all backend business code in this repository.
The frontend repository contains the project's Vue client code. Develop all frontend code in this repository.
The API repository contains all of the project's Java interface definitions. Develop all interface definitions in this repository.
The middleware repository contains all of the project's Java database and Redis operations. Develop all database and Redis code in this repository.

Repository relationships:
The frontend repository depends on the backend repository.
The backend repository depends on the API and middleware repositories.
```

This step defines the project's repositories, relationships, and development boundaries and associates them with Agents. Agents can then pull branches from the right repositories for development, testing, and deployment.

#### Configure MCP for Agents

Configure the CodeFlow platform MCP for Agents so each Agent can read platform information during execution. In “Personal settings”, create an MCP named “CodeFlow” and configure it in the current Workspace. Then ask the Agent to apply that MCP to all Agents. The prompt below asks it to configure the Workspace's “CodeFlow” MCP on every Agent and automatically publish and approve them afterward.

```markdown
Bind the "CodeFlow" MCP configured in my project Workspace to every Agent, then automatically publish and approve the Agents.
```





### Step 5: Validate the Delivery workflow

Before starting Delivery, ask the Agent to analyze whether the configuration is correct. The example asks it to examine the Agents, SDLC workflows, repositories, repository relationships, and Agent repository bindings in “Quick Delivery Squad”; determine whether automated Delivery can proceed; identify automatic stages and stages requiring human decisions; and provide the entire Delivery workflow as a Markdown flowchart. It also asks that `Soul.md` and `Agent.md` contain only shared Agent information, while information needed only by a specific SDLC step belongs in that step rather than all being placed in `Agent.md`.

```markdown
Fully analyze whether the Agents, SDLC workflows, repositories, repository relationships, and Agent repository bindings in the Quick Delivery Squad of the current Workspace are correct. Can the current configuration deliver a requirement automatically? Which stages run automatically, and which require human decisions? Provide the entire Delivery workflow as a Markdown flowchart.
Note: Configure only shared Agent information in Soul.md and Agent.md. Put information needed only by a specific SDLC step in that step's configuration, rather than putting all information in Agent.md.
```

Review the Agent's findings and decide whether further improvements are needed. The workflow configuration is central: its correctness directly determines whether Delivery completes as expected.

### Step 6: Prepare the runtime and register Executors

#### Install the CLI and plugins

On the machine where you will register Executors, download and install Agent CLI of your choice (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor CLI or Gemini CLI) and the SuperPowers plugin. You can use your own computer for initial trials; for stable operation, use a machine that can run continuously, such as a Linux server, desktop, or Mac mini. Get the CLI installation command from the official site of the client you choose, install the CLI, and configure its environment variables. Alternatively, give the installation command to an Agent and ask it to install the CLI and configure the environment variables, replacing `xxx` with the actual command.

```markdown
Install Claude Code CLI using this command and configure its environment variables. Installation command: xxx
```

After installation, run `claude` in the terminal (or the matching command for your client) and sign in. Then ask the CLI to install SuperPowers. Clarification uses SuperPowers to clarify requirements and generate Agent-oriented Spec and Plan files. If you already use a plugin such as OpenSpec, you can install that instead, but also update the instructions in the Requirements Clarification Agent's `Agent.md`. We recommend SuperPowers based on practices used by many enterprises. The example asks for a user-level installation from the official plugin address `https://github.com/obra/superpowers`.
```markdown
Install the SuperPowers plugin at the user level. Official plugin URL: https://github.com/obra/superpowers
```

#### Register and start Executors

Ask your Agent to configure Executors for all Agents in “Quick Delivery Squad” and for the Requirements Clarification Agent. Adjust the prompt for the client you actually use. The example specifies Claude CLI (or another supported client), platform memory, the latest Qwen flagship model for Clarification (for example `Qwen3.8-Max`), the latest Qwen Flash model for other Agents (the original example spells it `Qwne3.8-Flash`), `Medium` reasoning effort, a `1M` context window, and Executor names formed from “NO1” plus the Agent name. It then asks for every Executor's startup command in an `ainative-executor` script on the desktop supporting `start`, `stop`, and `status`.

```markdown
Configure Executors for every Agent in the Quick Delivery Squad and for the Requirements Clarification Agent:
- Select Claude CLI as the client type (Codex CLI, Cursor CLI and Gemini CLI are also supported; pick the one you actually use).
- Use platform memory.
- Use the latest Qwen flagship model for Requirements Clarification, such as Qwen3.8-Max. Use the latest Qwen Flash model for the other Agents, such as Qwne3.8-Flash.
- Select Medium reasoning effort.
- Select a 1M context window.
- Name each Executor using "NO1" plus the Agent name.

After configuring the Executors, retrieve all their startup commands and package them in a script named ainative-executor on my desktop. The script must support start, stop, and status commands.
```

Run the generated script on your computer or server to register Executors, then check the “Executors” page to confirm they are online.



## First Requirement Delivery

Configuration is now complete. Create a Requirement to try Delivery. There are two steps:
- Clarification.
- Start the task.

### Step 1

Start Clarification. The Agent uses the requirement and latest code to clarify it with you. At the last step, it presents the proposed design for confirmation. After you confirm, it generates `spec.md` and `plan.md` and uploads them as Requirement attachments. If the design needs changes, continue providing feedback until it meets your requirements, then confirm it.

**Note:** For Clarification, select **“Standard Automated Delivery Squad”**, which contains the Requirements Clarification Agent, then select the **“Requirements Clarification”** Agent and start.

![Clarification conversation](/help/assets/06-en-US.png "")



### Step 2

Return to the Requirement and start Delivery with the “Quick Full-Stack Developer” Agent in “Quick Delivery Squad”. If you later configure other Delivery Squads, choose the appropriate Squad. In the Quick Delivery template, the full-stack development Agent automatically hands off to “Quick Deployment Engineer” for deployment after development and testing finish.



![Start Delivery](/help/assets/09-en-US.png "")

Your first project is now onboarded and its first Delivery has started. Subsequent users only need to create a Requirement → clarify requirements → start Delivery.

In “Member management”, search by username to add teammates to this project Workspace and assign their permissions. There are three access levels:
- **Read only:** View project information without performing operations.
- **Read and write:** Create Requirements, perform Clarification, and start Requirements.
- **Administrator:** Manage project configuration, including Squads, Agents, SDLC workflows, repositories, and Executors.



Refer to “Practice cases” and continue refining the AI automated Delivery pipeline to fit your project.

title: Practice cases
markdown:
## **Performance testing platform (Web load-testing tool)**

- Requirement #10047 · 50 minutes · completed the four-step SDLC (analysis & branch preparation → coding & testing → verification & delivery → handover review)
- Requirement: a web tool that developers and testers can run load tests against themselves and inspect metric distributions

**Deliverables**

- `app.py` 788 lines (backend: ThreadingHTTPServer + hand-written minimal routing + load engine + JSON persistence), `index.html` 653 lines (single-file vanilla JS frontend, zero build, zero CDN)
- Python 3 **standard library only** — `pip install` was never executed
- Fixed port 8811, started with `python3 app.py`

**Verified results (actually executed)**

- 20 concurrent × 50 real requests: **50/50 succeeded, QPS 1975.77, 0 errors**
- All seven metrics present: QPS, average latency, P50, P95, P99, max latency, success rate and error count; `samples` records every request duration so the frontend can draw a latency histogram
- Live progress is visible: 53/3000 → 1045/3000 → 2049/3000
- GET / POST / HEAD are all load-testable

**A real defect found during delivery**

Python's `socketserver` default accept backlog is only 5, so 20 concurrent connections overflowed it and the kernel reset 36 of the 50 requests (`[Errno 54] Connection reset by peer`) — the success rate was down to 28%. A custom `PerfHTTPServer(ThreadingHTTPServer)` with `request_queue_size = 512` brought the success rate back to **100%**.

## **E-commerce site (Cloud Selection Mall)**

- Requirement #10049 · 20 minutes · completed the four-step SDLC
- Requirement: a full e-commerce loop with both a storefront and an admin console

**Deliverables**

- Single service, Node.js ≥ 18 running a single-process `node:http` server, **zero third-party runtime dependencies** (no dependencies in `package.json`)
- Server-rendered HTML + vanilla CSS, no build step and no external CDN, so it works offline; port 8802
- Storage prefers Node's built-in `node:sqlite` (`data/shop.db`, WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL`) and automatically falls back to a JSON file on Node < 22.5 (temp file + atomic rename), so **no external database service is required**
- Session: the cart lives on the server, identified by an HttpOnly `sid` cookie (7 days); browsers never share a cart

**Verified results (actually executed)**

- Storefront: product grid (cards / category filter / keyword search), product detail, add to cart, cart management (change quantity / remove / live total), checkout with receiver, phone and address validation, order confirmation page, order status and detail lookup by order number, and cancel of a pending order (rolling stock back)
- Admin console (separate path `/admin`): overview statistics, product listing / delisting, price and stock editing, order list filtered by status, and the shipping status transition
- Full loop verified: browse → add to cart → place order (order NO202611120555218625) → ship from the admin console → **shipped** ✓
- Transactions and idempotency: placing an order runs validation, stock deduction and order creation inside a single transaction that rolls back as a whole; cancelling rolls stock back too; seed data (10 products / 4 categories) is written on first start and never overwrites existing data

## **Teacher desk**

- V2.0 · 2026-11-13 · port **8812** (8811 belongs to the performance testing platform, the two are isolated)
- Requirement: a teaching management desk for classes, students, assignments, grades and entry history

**Deliverables**

- Python 3 **standard library only** plus a single-file vanilla JS frontend (zero build, zero CDN), started with `python3 app.py`
- 7 functional modules: class management, student management (nested under a class), courses and assignments, grade entry, grade lookup, overview dashboard and data persistence; 12 routes

**Verified results (actually executed)**

- Main chain connected end to end: create class → add students → create assignment → enter grades → look up grades
- Constraints behave as designed: student numbers are unique within a class (duplicates return 409), due dates must be `YYYY-MM-DD`, out-of-range scores return 400 and **the whole batch is not persisted**
- Grade conversion: 92→excellent, 85→good, 78→fair, 55→fail, and 45/50 = 90%→excellent
- The overview returns class / student / assignment / grade counts, the average score and the latest 5 entries in one call
- Data is identical after a restart; cascading deletes leave no orphans (deleting a class removes its assignments, deleting a student removes their grades)
- Concurrency safe: 100 concurrent requests with 0 failures, class ids unique, `(assignment, student)` pairs unique, no `.tmp` leftovers

**The same defect, for the second time**

Under concurrency the connections were reset again (34 of 40 failed). This time it was traced directly to `socketserver.TCPServer.request_queue_size` defaulting to only 5; a custom `AppServer(ThreadingHTTPServer)` with `request_queue_size = 128` fixed it.

## **What these three deliveries taught us**

1. **Smoke first**: before recording anything formal, run one 10-minute requirement through the whole chain — clarification → dispatch → artifacts → write-back — then start the formal recording. Both early products started that way.
2. **Deliverables must run with zero dependencies**: all three products are "clone and run" — no package installs from the network, no external database service; whoever picks them up starts them with `python3 app.py` / `node server.js`.
3. **Acceptance must be reproducible**: every case ships a `TEST.md` with real commands and real output rather than "it looked right"; QPS, P95, success rate and case counts are all measured values.
4. **Finding real defects during delivery is normal**: the performance platform and the teacher desk hit the same concurrency trap (Python's accept backlog overwhelmed); fixing it and re-running is what counts — never ship with a known defect.
5. **Executors and accounts**: during the early phase register one executor per digital worker on one machine; too many executors spread scheduling across machines, and a sleeping or powered-off machine then interrupts the flow. Move to 7×24 servers once you go to production. Sign in with personal accounts so audit logs identify who did what, grant platform admin rights to individual accounts on demand, and do not hand out project admin rights to everyone.
6. **Cost**: deterministic tasks are fine on a Flash model, while clarification and code review — the steps that decide delivery quality — deserve a flagship model; schedule non-urgent requirements in low-traffic windows to cut Credits consumption.

title: Frequently asked questions
markdown:
Q: I cannot see the detailed Delivery process in CodeFlow and feel uncertain. What should I focus on?

A: CodeFlow's AI Native SDLC changes software Delivery fundamentally compared with Vibe Coding. Agents handle the entire requirement Delivery process using the preconfigured workflow. People focus on Clarification and acceptance of the final results rather than every intermediate detail. This frees people to work on higher-value system architecture, business architecture, and business functionality, and allows one person to drive Delivery of multiple requirements in parallel.

Q: Our team wants to keep separate product, development, and testing roles. How should we configure Delivery?

A: Teams moving to full-stack development can use one Squad to deliver the whole requirement. Teams retaining traditional role-based work can design separate Squads, Agents, and SDLC workflows for their needs. Each role uses its own Squad to complete its part around the same Requirement, then reaches a human decision stage. You can also specify the downstream people in the SDLC workflow; they receive an IM notification and continue Delivery using their own Squad. Once the platform's IM tool is configured, hand off to the relevant user's registered username in the SDLC workflow to send collaboration notifications. You can also manually @mention a person in Requirement comments and ask them to take over the next stages.

Q: What should I do if a Requirement encounters an error during Delivery?

A: @mention the relevant Agent and ask what went wrong and how to resolve it. A desktop Agent connected to CodeFlow MCP can also analyze the Requirement's error. If you suspect a platform issue, connect the Agent to the CodeFlow source to investigate. If it confirms a platform defect, report the analysis to the platform maintainers for a fix.

Q: How many Requirements can one Executor run at once, and when should I add capacity?

A: By default, each Executor for each Agent can run up to ten tasks concurrently; additional tasks queue. Because each Requirement's workflow runs serially, a Squad's registered Executors can be understood as handling ten Requirements at a time. If your computer or server has enough capacity, you can register multiple sets of Executors on one machine. Each task uses an isolated session, so tasks do not interfere even on the same machine. When load becomes too high, add another machine and register Executors there; the platform will schedule new tasks to it. Executors are stateless and can scale horizontally, for example by adding multiple Mac mini machines to the same project for Delivery.

Q: How should we configure project knowledge bases and development standards?

A: For business logic already expressed in code, we do not recommend maintaining a separate knowledge base or explanation: code is the best documentation. For development standards or internal terminology, use one of these approaches:
1. Maintain the documents in source repositories. Specify in the Agent definition which repository content to read and at which stage.
2. Package the development standards as a Skill, upload it to CodeFlow, and bind it to the relevant Agents. Explain in each Agent definition when to use the Skill, which knowledge to retrieve, or which standards to follow.
3. Expose your internal knowledge base as a Skill or MCP, upload it to CodeFlow, and bind it to the relevant Agents. Update the Agent instructions to integrate the enterprise knowledge base.

Q: What should I do if a Requirement's workflow takes too long?

A: Consider these situations:
1. Execution time depends on the automated Delivery pipeline definition. A long workflow takes longer to complete.
2. Agent and SDLC definitions often have substantial room for improvement. Missing environment dependencies or imprecise workflow instructions can cause extra reasoning and retries, wasting time and Credits. Use an Agent to analyze and improve the definitions continuously. Also use the platform's workflow optimization capabilities to identify and improve pipeline configuration.
3. Replace model reasoning with scripts wherever scripts can accomplish the work.

CodeFlow's AI Native SDLC is a form of software Delivery for the AI era. People clarify requirements and make decisions; the automated pipeline handles the connecting and manual work that previously required people. You can focus on requirements and results instead of watching every execution step.

Focus on whether Delivery quality meets requirements, whether the automated production pipeline runs efficiently in the current environment, and whether Credit optimization meets your needs.

During working hours, people and Agents deliver requirements together. At night, Agents continue Delivery using Scheduled tasks and the automated pipeline, and you accept the results the next day. This enables 7×24-hour Delivery, with one person driving continuous Delivery of multiple requirements in parallel.

Q: What should I do if Delivery quality does not meet requirements?

A: Improve the automated pipeline for the specific problems. Use unit, integration, E2E, feature, and Playwright tests to protect quality. Add development standards and requirements to the pipeline through Skills, project documents, and similar mechanisms.

Q: What should I do if the frontend does not match the intended design closely enough?

A: Try these approaches:
1. Define frontend development standards, including element colors, spacing, and pagination styles, to improve quality.
2. Confirm the frontend design as HTML, then upload the HTML to the Requirement so subsequent development can build directly from it. Design and confirmation of the HTML can be stages in the automated Delivery pipeline; arrange the workflow as needed.

markdown:
## Preview & Download

The complete product manual is available as a PDF — great for printing, offline reading, or onboarding new team members.

[User Manual — codeflow-user-manual-v2.1.1.pdf](/help/assets/codeflow-user-manual-v2.1.1.pdf)

- **Open preview**: browse it right in the browser;
- **Download PDF**: save a copy for printing or offline reading.

The manual ends with a “Support & Contact” section — WeChat QR code (note codeflow) for deployment questions, source access and troubleshooting. The manual matches this documentation center (baseline v2.1.0, 2026-11-17). If anything differs from the actual UI, the running product wins — feedback via Issues is welcome.
